architectural_implications.after: All requests route through an audited gateway that unwraps JWE tokens and enforces identity.
architectural_implications.before: Agents or clients connect directly to backend APIs and MCP servers.
architectural_implications.consequence: Access control and audit centralize at the gateway; direct server exposure and shadow IT become detectable and blockable.
architectural_implications.observation: Tool access is mediated by a gateway that carries real identity, with MCP servers hidden behind it.

architectural_implications.after: Context is selected, reranked, deduplicated, and compressed before ingestion.
architectural_implications.before: Full retrieved context is passed to the model, with cost managed by prompt tweaks.
architectural_implications.consequence: Token cost becomes an engineered, measurable pipeline output rather than an emergent expense.
architectural_implications.observation: A dedicated context optimizer layer sits between context assembly and the LLM.

architectural_implications.after: OTel collectors route traces to Tempo, metrics to Prometheus, and quality/job data to BigQuery.
architectural_implications.before: A single logging path conflates model behavior with infrastructure events.
architectural_implications.consequence: Quality evaluation and infrastructure debugging get independent, queryable pipelines.
architectural_implications.observation: Telemetry is split into agent-side LLM signals and gateway operational signals.

architectural_implications.after: Write and sensitive actions branch through an execute-vs-reject approval diamond.
architectural_implications.consequence: Catastrophic autonomous modifications are bounded, at the cost of workflow latency and human load.
architectural_implications.observation: High-risk actions are gated by an explicit HITL approval node in the agent graph.

connections.connects_to: OAuth authentication and JWE access tokens
connections.relationship: The gateway uses OAuth-derived, JWE-wrapped tokens to establish real identity and unwraps them centrally, making identity the enforcement primitive for tool access.
Both are context-supply layers: checkpoints restore workflow state while the optimizer prunes and compresses the working context before LLM ingestion.
Separating agent-side from gateway telemetry enables independent quality evaluation tables and infrastructure metrics from the same OTLP stream.
Both constrain agent autonomy at different layers: HITL gates high-risk actions at runtime, while typed tool scoping removes dangerous actions from the callable surface entirely.

evidence_quotes.text: MCP gateway ensures every request runs as a real identity through an audited gateway
MCP servers never face the client directly

core_insights.generalization: For any tool-using agent system, insert a policy/identity enforcement layer between the agent runtime and backend APIs so authorization and audit live outside the LLM's control.
core_insights.insight: The MCP gateway functions as a mandatory identity-bearing chokepoint: every agent tool call is authenticated as a real user identity and passes through an audited gateway with JWE access-token un-wrapping, and MCP servers are never exposed directly to clients.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Reframes MCP from a developer-convenience protocol into a security boundary; it eliminates shadow IT and unauthenticated LLM tool invocations, and makes the gateway — not the agent — the unit of access control and audit.

evidence_quotes.text: MCP servers enforce request filters, limits, and blocked fields
MCP turns REST APIs into safe, agent-friendly tools

core_insights.generalization: Constrain agent capability by narrowing the callable API surface (typed args, hard limits, blocked fields) instead of relying on prompt instructions or output validation alone.
core_insights.insight: Wrapping REST APIs with FastMCP exposes typed, permission-scoped tools with request filters, limits, and blocked fields, reviewed by security before production, so the LLM cannot construct arbitrary or dangerous API calls.
core_insights.why_it_matters: The tool surface, not the prompt, becomes the enforcement point for API safety; constraints are declared at the schema/tool boundary rather than trusted to model behavior.

evidence_quotes.text: Context optimization saves 70% to 90% in token costs
Demo showed token usage dropping from 24,000 tokens down to 2,400 tokens (90% savings) for the same query.

core_insights.generalization: Treat context construction as an optimizing pipeline (select/rerank/dedup/compress) with token-cost as a first-class metric to be benchmarked per query class.
core_insights.insight: A context optimizer that selects relevant payloads, reranks, deduplicates, and compresses context before LLM ingestion cut token usage from 24,000 to 2,400 for the same query (90% reduction).
core_insights.why_it_matters: Demonstrates a concrete, measurable cost lever for high-volume agents, with the optimizer positioned as its own layer rather than a side effect of prompt engineering.

evidence_quotes.text: Separate agent-side LLM telemetry from gateway operational telemetry
BigQuery tables: agent_job_tracking, agent_quality_eval, agent_tool_invocations

core_insights.generalization: Instrument agent semantics (quality, tool invocations, eval scores) separately from infrastructure operations (gateway latency, errors) so each can be owned and queried independently.
core_insights.insight: Agent-side LLM telemetry is deliberately separated from gateway operational telemetry, with OpenTelemetry collectors routing traces to Tempo and metrics to Prometheus, plus BigQuery tables for job tracking and quality evaluation.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Splitting the two signal domains lets teams do root-cause analysis on agent reasoning/quality independently from infrastructure latency and reliability, which is hard when both are conflated in one pipeline.

evidence_quotes.text: PII trimming blocks high-severity secrets from ever reaching LLMs
Blocking private keys, AWS access keys, SSNs, credit cards with 95%+ severity rules

core_insights.generalization: Place a deterministic, severity-thresholded redaction layer on the ingestion path ahead of any model or logging sink.
core_insights.insight: A real-time PII trimmer blocks high-severity secrets (private keys, AWS access keys, SSNs, credit cards) using 95%+ severity rules before anything reaches the LLM or tracking systems.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Moves data protection upstream of the model and of the observability stack, so leaked secrets cannot propagate into prompts, traces, or eval datasets.

evidence_quotes.text: Dev portal creates repository with workload identity, memory DB, tracking tables, and secret management automatically.

core_insights.generalization: Encode agent production requirements (identity, persistence, telemetry, secrets) into a golden-path scaffold so compliance is automatic and uniform.
core_insights.insight: A dev portal auto-scaffolds each new agent with workload identity, a memory DB, tracking tables, and secret management, standardizing deployment across the whole engineering org.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Shifts governance from per-team discipline to platform-provided defaults, making production controls the path of least resistance rather than optional add-ons.

SQLite for local development, Cloud Spanner for production

core_insights.insight: Agent persistence uses thread IDs and checkpoints for durability across runs, with SQLite for local development and Cloud Spanner for production.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Checkpointing gives seamless recovery and continuity for long-running workflows, and the local/prod backend split lets developers iterate without provisioning production state stores.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Harish Gaggar
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Building and governing enterprise AI agents for production deployment
  • Purpose: To provide engineers and enterprise architects with a comprehensive framework and architectural blueprint for deploying secure, auditable, and cost-efficient AI agents in production. Harish Gaggar, Senior Staff Software Engineer at Credit Karma, explains how to transition AI agents from experiments to secure, governed enterprise production environments. He covers architectural patterns, MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers and gateways, monitoring, tracking and evaluation, PII blocking, and context optimization.

Topic Map

Challenges in Enterprise AI Agents

  • Explanation: Enterprise AI agents often fail in production because foundational controls such as gateways, proper tool execution, tracking, memory management, and security are missing.
  • Key claims:
    • AI agents fail in production when foundational controls are missing
    • Many lack secure gateways for authentication and authorization
    • Missing tracking, memory management, and PII data blocking
  • Examples:
    • Secrets leaking into LLMs or tracking systems
    • Lack of audit trails for agent tool executions
  • Terminology:
    • foundational controls
    • gateway
    • MCP gateway
  • Why it matters: Without proper enterprise controls, AI agents pose severe security, privacy, and cost risks in production.

Design Framework for Enterprise Agents

  • Explanation: A layered framework encompassing agent frameworks, OAuth authentication, customized MCP servers, continuous audit, PII stripping, tracking and eval, memory management, and context optimization.
  • Key claims:
    • Each layer must be scoped, sanitized, audited, and measured by design
    • An agent needs an enterprise-grade framework around it, not just a standalone agent
  • Examples:
    • LangGraph for task-specific nodes, skills, and prompts
    • FastMCP wrapper for exposing typed tools
  • Terminology:
    • agent framework
    • FastMCP
    • HITL
    • context optimizer
  • Why it matters: Structured layering ensures safety, compliance, and predictable behavior at enterprise scale.

MCP Servers and Gateways

  • Explanation: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers turn REST APIs into typed, permission-scoped tools, while MCP gateways provide centralized authentication, routing, and JWE access token un-wrapping.
  • Key claims:
    • MCP servers enforce request filters, limits, and blocked fields
    • MCP gateway ensures every request runs as a real identity through an audited gateway
    • MCP servers never face the client directly
  • Examples:
    • Artifactory MCP and GitHub MCP
    • Redis session state storage for OAuth requests
  • Terminology:
    • MCP server
    • MCP gateway
    • FastMCP
    • JWE access token
  • Why it matters: Decoupling clients from servers via a secure gateway prevents unauthorized direct access to enterprise data and internal tools.

Monitoring, Tracking, and Evaluation

  • Explanation: Comprehensive telemetry using OpenTelemetry collectors, Tempo for traces, Prometheus for metrics, and Grafana for dashboards, alongside BigQuery tables for agent job tracking and evaluation.
  • Key claims:
    • AI agents cannot be trusted without continuous monitoring, evaluation, and feedback
    • Separate agent-side LLM telemetry from gateway operational telemetry
  • Examples:
    • BigQuery tables: agent_job_tracking, agent_quality_eval, agent_tool_invocations
    • OpenTelemetry collector routing to Tempo and Prometheus
  • Terminology:
    • OpenTelemetry
    • Tempo
    • Prometheus
    • Grafana
    • OTLP
  • Why it matters: Enables root cause analysis, latency tracking, cost monitoring, and quality evaluation across hundreds of deployed agents.

Agent Memory, PII Blocking, and Context Optimization

  • Explanation: Persistent checkpointing for workflows across runs, real-time PII stripping before LLM ingestion, and a context optimizer to prune, rerank, and compress context to save token costs.
  • Key claims:
    • Agent persistence ensures durability and seamless recovery across runs using thread IDs and checkpoints
    • PII trimming blocks high-severity secrets from ever reaching LLMs
    • Context optimization saves 70% to 90% in token costs
  • Examples:
    • SQLite for local development, Cloud Spanner for production
    • Blocking private keys, AWS access keys, SSNs, credit cards with 95%+ severity rules
  • Terminology:
    • checkpointing
    • thread ID
    • PII trimmer
    • context optimizer
    • token savings
  • Why it matters: Protects sensitive enterprise data from leaking while drastically reducing LLM operational costs.

Key Points

Build an enterprise framework, not just an AI agent

  • Explanation: Production agents require surrounding infrastructure for registration, CI/CD pipelines, secret management, memory, and tracking.
  • Evidence: Dev portal creates repository with workload identity, memory DB, tracking tables, and secret management automatically.
  • Practical implication: Standardizes agent development and deployment across the entire engineering organization.

Gateway-first security is the foundation

  • Explanation: All tool calls must be authenticated and governed through an MCP gateway before reaching backend servers.
  • Evidence: Architecture diagrams show MCP servers never facing clients directly; all requests pass through the gateway with JWE tokens.
  • Practical implication: Eliminates shadow IT and unauthenticated LLM tool invocations.

MCP turns REST APIs into safe, agent-friendly tools

  • Explanation: Using FastMCP server wrappers, developers expose typed, permission-scoped tools with strict input filters and limits.
  • Evidence: Internal security teams review all tools before deployment to production.
  • Practical implication: Prevents LLMs from constructing arbitrary or dangerous API calls.

Keep humans in control of high-risk actions

  • Explanation: Write and sensitive operations must pass through Human-In-The-Loop (HITL) approval workflows.
  • Evidence: Agent framework flow includes approval diamond checking execute vs reject states.
  • Practical implication: Mitigates catastrophic errors or unintended modifications by autonomous agents.

Optimize context before it becomes cost

  • Explanation: Context optimizers select relevant payloads, rerank information, remove duplicates, and compress prompts before sending to LLMs.
  • Evidence: Demo showed token usage dropping from 24,000 tokens down to 2,400 tokens (90% savings) for the same query.
  • Practical implication: Enormous reduction in API costs for high-volume enterprise AI agents.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Agent Design & Governance Framework

  • How it works: A multi-layered architecture handling requests from agent framework through OAuth, MCP gateway, customized servers, PII stripping, tracking, memory, and context optimization.
  • Components:
    • Agent Framework (LangGraph)
    • OAuth Authentication
    • Customized MCP Server
    • Continuous Audit
    • PII/Secrets Stripping
    • Tracking and Evaluation
    • Memory Management
    • Context Optimizer
  • When to use: When deploying multi-agent workflows into enterprise production environments.

Context Optimizer Framework

  • How it works: Selects payload based on token limit, reranks relevant information, clusters to remove duplicates, and compresses the final context before LLM invocation.
  • Components:
    • Select
    • Rerank
    • Cluster
    • Compress
  • When to use: When handling large codebases, documentation, or extensive tool outputs to avoid token bloat and high costs.

Examples & Case Studies

Running a supply chain agent query searching for vulnerable Docker images across repositories in Artifactory.

  • Illustrates: How agent tracking, eval tables, and tool invocations record metrics and trajectories in BigQuery.
  • Lesson: Granular logging allows deep auditing of every LLM call, token usage, latency, and tool success rate.

Executing a complex query with and without the Context Optimizer enabled.

  • Illustrates: Token usage dropping from ~24,000 tokens to ~2,400 tokens (~90% cost savings).
  • Lesson: Context optimization preserves output quality while dramatically reducing token consumption.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Implement gateway-first authentication for all agent tool calls
    • Adopt FastMCP for building typed, secure MCP servers
    • Deploy PII and secret trimming before data reaches LLMs
  • Strategic:
    • Build a centralized developer portal for registering and deploying governed agents
    • Establish rigorous tracking, evaluation, and telemetry using OpenTelemetry and BigQuery
    • Always include Human-In-The-Loop approval gates for write and sensitive operations
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do we scale MCP gateways across multi-cloud enterprise environments?
    • What are the latency tradeoffs of running multi-layer PII filters and context optimizers?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Context optimizers can save 70% to 90% in token costs while maintaining agent accuracy (performance metric)
  • MCP servers combined with MCP gateways completely eliminate unauthenticated LLM tool execution (architectural claim)

Notable Quotes

"Enterprise AI agents often fail in production when foundational controls are missing" (at 2:09) "MCP server is a protocol layer that turns REST API into typed, permission-scoped tools an agent can safely call" (at 13:36) "Every request runs as a real identity through audited gateway" (at 26:49)

Compressed Summary

  • Enterprise AI agents require robust architectural controls, not just standalone code
  • MCP servers and gateways enforce strict authentication, routing, and tool scoping
  • Memory management via thread checkpointing ensures workflow durability and recovery
  • PII strippers block sensitive secrets from reaching LLMs and logging backends
  • Context optimizers cut token consumption by up to 90% through select, rerank, cluster, and compress
  • Keywords: mcp, gateway, governance, agents, telemetry, optimization
  • Core insight: Production-grade enterprise AI agents require gateway-first security, protocol-based tool servers (MCP), rigorous tracking, and context optimization to ensure safety, auditability, and cost efficiency.

  - Agent persistence ensures durability and seamless recovery across runs using thread IDs and checkpoints
  - PII trimming blocks high-severity secrets from ever reaching LLMs
  - Context optimization saves 70% to 90% in token costs
- **Examples**:
  - SQLite for local development, Cloud Spanner for production
  - Blocking private keys, AWS access keys, SSNs, credit cards with 95%+ severity rules
- **Terminology**:
  - checkpointing
  - thread ID
  - PII trimmer
  - context optimizer
  - token savings
- **Why it matters**: Protects sensitive enterprise data from leaking while drastically reducing LLM operational costs.
## Key Points
### Build an enterprise framework, not just an AI agent
- **Explanation**: Production agents require surrounding infrastructure for registration, CI/CD pipelines, secret management, memory, and tracking.
- **Evidence**: Dev portal creates repository with workload identity, memory DB, tracking tables, and secret management automatically.
- **Practical implication**: Standardizes agent development and deployment across the entire engineering organization.
### Gateway-first security is the foundation
- **Explanation**: All tool calls must be authenticated and governed through an MCP gateway before reaching backend servers.
- **Evidence**: Architecture diagrams show MCP servers never facing clients directly; all requests pass through the gateway with JWE tokens.
- **Practical implication**: Eliminates shadow IT and unauthenticated LLM tool invocations.
### MCP turns REST APIs into safe, agent-friendly tools
- **Explanation**: Using FastMCP server wrappers, developers expose typed, permission-scoped tools with strict input filters and limits.
- **Evidence**: Internal security teams review all tools before deployment to production.
- **Practical implication**: Prevents LLMs from constructing arbitrary or dangerous API calls.
### Keep humans in control of high-risk actions
- **Explanation**: Write and sensitive operations must pass through Human-In-The-Loop (HITL) approval workflows.
- **Evidence**: Agent framework flow includes approval diamond checking execute vs reject states.
- **Practical implication**: Mitigates catastrophic errors or unintended modifications by autonomous agents.
### Optimize context before it becomes cost
- **Explanation**: Context optimizers select relevant payloads, rerank information, remove duplicates, and compress prompts before sending to LLMs.
- **Evidence**: Demo showed token usage dropping from 24,000 tokens down to 2,400 tokens (90% savings) for the same query.
- **Practical implication**: Enormous reduction in API costs for high-volume enterprise AI agents.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Agent Design & Governance Framework
- **How it works**: A multi-layered architecture handling requests from agent framework through OAuth, MCP gateway, customized servers, PII stripping, tracking, memory, and context optimization.
- **Components**:
  - Agent Framework (LangGraph)
  - OAuth Authentication
  - Customized MCP Server
  - Continuous Audit
  - PII/Secrets Stripping
  - Tracking and Evaluation
  - Memory Management
  - Context Optimizer
- **When to use**: When deploying multi-agent workflows into enterprise production environments.
### Context Optimizer Framework
- **How it works**: Selects payload based on token limit, reranks relevant information, clusters to remove duplicates, and compresses the final context before LLM invocation.
- **Components**:
  - Select
  - Rerank
  - Cluster
  - Compress
- **When to use**: When handling large codebases, documentation, or extensive tool outputs to avoid token bloat and high costs.
## Examples & Case Studies

## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Implement gateway-first authentication for all agent tool calls
  - Adopt FastMCP for building typed, secure MCP servers
  - Deploy PII and secret trimming before data reaches LLMs
- **Strategic**:

  - Establish rigorous tracking, evaluation, and telemetry using OpenTelemetry and BigQuery
  - Always include Human-In-The-Loop approval gates for write and sensitive operations

- Context optimizers can save 70% to 90% in token costs while maintaining agent accuracy (performance metric)
- MCP servers combined with MCP gateways completely eliminate unauthenticated LLM tool execution (architectural claim)
